It will be difficult to find, not only in Christian literature, but not even in universal literature, a more beautiful and charming, more exciting and suggestive book, after the Holy Bible, than the Confessions of Saint Augustine. Because although all those who came out of his wonderful pen are admirable, and we would almost say divine, among them, however, shines among them, like a gem of unusual brilliance, this fascinating and original book of his, which for fifteen centuries has not ceased to be read with supreme delight by the wise and the ignorant, by the credulous and the unbelievers. The Saint himself already speaks to us, not without a certain author's satisfaction, of the success and applause with which he was received by his faithful and friends when he gave it to public light for the first time. «What book is there of mine—he writes in De dono perseverantiae—that is read more frequently and with more delight than that of my Confessions? * And in book II of the Retractions: «I know that my Confessions have pleased and please many of my brothers very much.» And the centuries, without interruption or discrepancies, have confirmed precisely this flattering judgment of their contemporaries. Even in our days, so cultured and so demanding in their literary tastes, what book is there that is read with more frequency and delight, with more charm and benefit, not only by good and spiritual souls, but even by men of letters and refined tasters of pure aesthetic beauty? And yet, it must be recognized, literary speaking and in a classicist sense, perhaps this is not the most perfect work that came out of his hands nor perhaps even the most brilliant and grandiose. But he has put into it so much that is personal and living, so much that is dynamic and emotional, that from the first pages, despite the heavy and long philosophical digressions to which he frequently indulges, it subjugates and enthralls, until it completely takes over the reader. That's why this book is everyone's book. In it we all find an unmistakable piece of our being, a bleeding piece of our heart, a shred of our intimate and confidential life, and often not of what is most vile and despicable in it. Apart from other things, there is no doubt that this is one of the main secrets of the attractive force of this wonderful book, the first of its kind and which still does not have a second. Because it is not precisely the story of a man's sins that excites our curiosity in this book, nor is it the wonderful art of describing certain states of the soul, nor the psychic process of a labored and painful conversion, nor the subtle analyzes of the hidden movements of the human heart, always versatile and protean, refractory to itself and any concrete formula of being. No; This is not what attracts and suggests us in this book, being all this and much more. Also in the Confessions of Rousseau, a poor imitation of those of Augustine, one finds magnificent paintings, wonderfully chiseled literary pages, profound analyzes of human passions, stories of sins more vile and gross than those of Augustine; but its pages are dead pages that fall from the hands, that leave the soul dry and suggest nothing more than disgust and disdain in the face of an unparalleled cynicism that, after covering itself in filth, has the arrogance to insult others, challenging them to raise their finger if they are better than him. In the Confessions of Saint Augustine, on the contrary, there is a breath of life, a flame of love that ignites in souls, and captivates and enamors them, and elevates and dignifies them, and transforms them and brings them closer to God. No book by the Holy Doctor raises so much—as he himself tells us—the soul and the heart towards God as this one of his Confessions. They are a hymn of glory, a rapturous song of love and gratitude "to the just and good God" for his mercies without number and his graces without measure, which cannot be read without being ignited by love and feeling as if carried away by the spirit of God, which warms all its parts and penetrates even its smallest cracks and syllables.

And, although we all see reflected in its pages our perverse background, what is in us of earth and silt, we also see what is good and holy, what is of heaven and God, and that, above our miseries and vileness, it struggles to rise above, to soar to the heights and rise to God himself. Here is the secret of the Confessions of the holy Bishop of Hippo. Book of strong reading, of countless suggestions, of supreme delight for great and noble souls. One and only book of its kind, as unique is the genius who conceived it and gave it being. Eternal book, which seems to renew and grow with the centuries. The most original, the most beautiful, the most intimate, the most vast and luminous and the most deeply meaningful book of those that have been written in human language by men. Poem of the soul, song of triumph and love with resonances of heaven and earth, with accents of holy emotion, which only divine grace composed and only with it is felt and perceived. Moan of a wounded turtledove, sigh of burning passion, roar of a prisoner lion, cry of triumph and victory of a soul that saves between life and death. All of this is the Confessions of Saint Augustine, and that is why reading it captivates and moves us, and ignites and burns us, and, like noble prisoners, it subjugates us and drags us with it in its ever ascending career towards God. But these are not only the Confessions of the great convert of Milan. It has always been the pleasure of mortal gods, of sublime and pure souls, of geniuses and privileged vates, the contemplation of the vast panoramas of the world, of the wonders of divine creation, whose harmonies and beauties speak to them with a language so ineffable and mysterious, so intimate and penetrating, so sublime and captivating, that, immersed in indescribable ecstasy, they seem to already feel close to themselves that supreme beauty, that sweet harmony that is of all First, that concert and universal rhythm that is the reason and measure of all things. But no matter how big, no matter how beautiful, no matter how splendid the world that surrounds us is with all its wonders and variety of elements, the world of souls is undoubtedly much greater, much more beautiful and sublime. And if it is about some chosen and privileged ones of God, like that of Saint Augustine, this vision goes up a notch, clothing an interest, a charm and spiritual delight with nothing comparable. And this is precisely what the Confessions are: a wonderful diorama of the soul of Saint Augustine. Saint Augustine has poured, so to speak, his entire soul into the Confessions.

We would become endless if we wanted to select only his lapidary phrases, his brilliant sentences, his apothegms of wonder, which have mostly passed into ordinary language or books of piety and religion. It would also be to tear such precious gems from the frame and place in which the great goldsmith set them with unsurpassed art, and in which they shine with their own brilliance and contrast, like the great colors of a master painting, which mutually reinforce and complete each other. Because that is also what Saint Augustine is: an unsurpassed and unique master in the art of painting human passions, both in their violent manifestations and harsh cuts as well as in their sweetest and most delicate notes, a philosopher by temperament, a subtle and penetrating analyst, a perpetual scrutinizer of the most hidden recesses of the mysterious human heart, a man of deep emotions and a fantasy, oriental, soul. vibrant and with multiple resonances, he has left us in this book of Confessions pictures so sovereignly drawn, so full of life and color, that those who come will strive in vain to try to surpass them or even equal them. Also extremely beautiful is the scene, full of tragic realism and palpitating emotion, of Augustine's escape to Rome, mocking his mother on the beach of Carthage, whom he abandons, leaving his heart pierced and half agonizing with pain. With what pain, with what delicate brushstrokes she describes to us the despair of that poor and unfortunate mother when she realized that she had been deceived and betrayed by that son whom she loved so much, so much and who owed her so much! Augustine depicts her as a prisoner of despair and delirium, screaming and running like a madwoman from one part of the beach to another, advancing on the sea as if she wanted to follow that cruel ship that was thus snatching away the pledge of her womb, until finally, exhausted and exhausted, she falls to her knees half fainting at the foot of the chapel of San Cipriano, calling him a liar and a bad son, although without stopping praying for him. Finally, admirable is the description he gives us of the drama of his conversion in the Milan garden, and more than admirable, sublime is the vision of Ostia, immortalized by the brush of Ary Scheffer, even if it is nothing more than a very pale reflection of it and in a fleeting moment of abandonment of the human. And who has been able to surpass the portraits he gives us of his mother, of his bosom friend, Alypius, of his disciples and confidants and even of his own adversaries, such as Faustus and the Manichaeans? Where Augustine puts his pen, it is difficult to say more or better. He knows how to reach the core of things with a trait and reveal the most hidden and mysterious of them; He knows how to bring to flower and in all its vitality the latent and vague concepts that lie imprecise in the depths of the subconscious; He knows how to give life to the most vulgar and faded facts; He, finally, knows how to mortally wound all his enemies with a word, undoing their sophistry and errors with the same ease with which a legendary warrior destroys the hosts of his adversaries. And Saint Augustine equally dominates the regions of thought and those of psychological analysis, the springs of feeling and those of the art of expression.

He lived life fully in its triple dimension and with all the intensity with which it can be lived, and from it he takes as his first source the immense richness of his metaphors and expressions, almost all of them new, lively, vibrant and bold and of unparalleled strength and color. Master in the art of forms, he frequently delights in breaking the classic and trite ones, to create new ones of his own stamp and mars, '= Conf. IV 4.9 and 6.11.

In the Confessions this type of expression abounds more than in all the works of the Holy Doctor put together. It seems that, always dissatisfied with himself and his word, he resorts to the most violent and contrasting metaphors to give full and turgid reality to his thoughts and the infinite and overflowing desires of his heart. That is why when he has found the happy formula, he flatters and caresses it with intentional delay and delights in it, and repeats and glosses it until making us feel it like a refrain of achieved perfection, which sticks to the soul and even to the sense. It would be a long task, and a particularly painful one, to want to extract all the beauties and literary charms that the Confessions contain. Not a simple preliminary note, but an entire book would be necessary for this. It would be necessary to analyze on each page, and sometimes even in each line, the various concepts and meanings with which his sentences are fraught; because no one like Saint Augustine has possessed the art of condensing in a few words worlds of ideas, complex visions of forms, vast and unknown panoramas, full of aporias, tremendous amounts of life and light. But, being long and painful, such a task would also be unnecessary. To read the Confessions fruitfully, to feel their sovereign beauties, more than exegetes and commentators, what is needed are delicate and sensitive souls, clean and healthy eyes, pure hearts and lovers of supreme beauty. Because, although Saint Augustine was a great rhetorician and writer, he spoke to us in such a simple language, so without secret or artifice, so intimate and natural, that even the most humble and rude of his peasant women or the last of his monks could understand it without effort. It is not science that speaks there, it is not the smell of cedars that is felt there: it is the language of the soul that prays and confesses there, it is the voice of the contrite and humiliated heart that groans and sighs there, sings and praises in the presence of God and men with the simplicity of a child and the sublimity of an angel.

Although the Confessions of Saint Augustine, considered as such, are, as we have said, a unique and unique work in the world, considered, however, as a simple autobiography, some antecedents could perhaps be pointed out, even if very remote and fragmentary and, as a general rule, of little literary value. And the fact is that the autobiographical genre was very little cultivated among the ancients, refractory to this type of writing, in which they saw nothing more than an excessive display of one's own person, a certain egotistical desire for notoriety or, at least, a vanity and glorification of one's own merits, which frequently, if not almost always, were of little interest except to themselves or their descendants. One of the great philosophers of Greece had said: «The wise man should never speak about himself, neither to humiliate himself nor to exalt himself; "Contempt and glory must be for him two worthless things that will never disturb his spirit." This is the reason for the sporadic, fragmentary and circumstantial nature of the few manifestations that pagan antiquity has left us of the autobiographical genre. History tells us, among the Romans, about Aemilius Scaurus 1, Sylla 2, Rutillo Rufus 3, Lutado Catullus 4, Varro 5, Marcus Aurelius 6 and Rutilius C. Namaciano \ But the biographical news that they have left us and that has reached us is so brief, so disjointed and disjointed, that one has to strain the imagination to see in them an autobiography of the author. They are appreciable notes, interesting personal references, loose data from an episodic life, fundamental and precious, if you will, but nothing that resembles a psychographic study, the intimate history of a soul that has suffered and traveled long for the conquest of the truth. And what could a soul of pagan antiquity offer to the contemplation of men but spiritual emptiness and misery, and inner ugliness, and self-satisfaction, and ambition without measure of glory and applause? But as precious as all these autobiographical writings are, when they are carefully compared with the Confessions of Saint Augustine, they appear so different, so different in length and merit, and even in their very literary structure, that they cannot really be considered precursors except in a very broad and benign sense. Say as much as you want, it is necessary to recognize that in its literary writing, in its doctrinal content, in its breadth and development, the Confessions of Saint Augustine do not recognize any precedent worth taking into account, much less that it could have been an occasional source of inspiration. The Confessions of Saint Augustine, as Harnack writes, constitute a unique literary genre, totally original and its own, which was born with the Hippo Doctor, and, like all the creations of genius, is born already perfect, complete, without amendments or touch-ups. A landmark work, totally new, both for the plan it develops and for the method it uses, the spirit that animates it and the language it uses. Saint Augustine had to improvise everything: genre, form and title. His work must have appeared as an extra and disconcerting novelty. In fact it was in every sense of the word.

A book so suggestive, so passionate, and so widely read, could not help but arouse imitators over the centuries. The great biographer of Saint Augustine, Saint Posidius of Calama, who lived with him in sweet harmony, absque ulla amaritudine, for nearly forty years; who sat at his table constantly and was the confidant of his heart and the witness of his most secret actions during that long period of time; who loved him dearly in life and cried for him like no one else in death, speaks to us like this when he comes to the Confessions—whose story he intended to continue—, wanting to point out the purpose for which the great Doctor composed them: "He wanted to do this (write the Confessions), as the Apostle says, so that no one among mortals would believe or think about him more than what he knew, which he was and claimed about himself, using in it the style proper to the saint." humility, not wanting to deceive anyone or seek his praise, but only that of his Lord, because of his liberation and the favors that the Lord had given him, and asking his brothers for prayers for which he still hoped to receive. Surely no one is better aware than Possidius of the occasional motives of the Confessions; His testimony must therefore be considered, due to the qualities that surround it, as a statement of an exceptional witness. And the Confessions and other testimonies of the Holy Doctor agree perfectly with Possidius. The one from the Epistle to Darius, which we have transcribed above, is already known. Likewise those of the Confessions, in which the concept of penitential satisfaction, of edification of the faithful or of praise to God is sometimes expressed too vividly, but in all of them there is the feeling of self-humiliation and spiritual dejection in the presence of God and men. And it is explained. When Augustine wrote his Confessions, he was already surrounded on all sides by cheers and applause. Glory and admiration accompanied him everywhere. Despite his past life, he had been elevated to the priesthood and quickly to the episcopacy. His writings, which continued incessantly, were received as almost divine oracles, being snatched from his desk even before being finished. Captain of the armies of the Lord, wherever he appeared, there the enemies of the name of Christ were defeated, sinking them, one after another, into the abyss of confusion and ignominy. He was the great hero of the divine cause, the great doctor and teacher not only of Africa, but of the universal Church. Augustine felt loved, and more than loved, idolized everywhere; He saw himself applauded, praised, exalted to the clouds. In human terms he could believe himself happy and satisfied. However, Augustine trembles and is frightened and seeks in the shelter of the sanctuary at the foot of the altar the shield that will protect him, the medicine that will heal him from the daily wounds he receives and the strength that will sustain him against the terrible enemy of vanity. Because, although holy, he has a heart of flesh and none of it is foreign to him. human weaknesses. "No est mihi cornea fiber," exclaims the great Doctor in anguish. And the praise and the applause and the worldly glory and vanity stick to him and enter him without feeling to the depths of his soul, and before he knows it they surprise and captivate him with their delight. If anyone has felt this temptation of vainglory and self-indulgence and the flattery of the popular aura in all its force, it was Augustine. But Augustine has received in his soul the fullness of divine illumination and knows that only God is good and praiseworthy and worthy of all honor and glory, and he also knows that man has nothing in him but sin, and misery, and darkness, and vanity, imperfection and insufficiency for good work, and that it would be absolutely nothing if he left him out of his hand. Augustine has also told us that he has been wounded by the dart of God's love and that he no longer wants anything for himself, but everything for God.

The mere thought that he can boast of the smallest divine gift or grace fills him with terror. That is why he groans and cries and is distressed when he sees that men look at the little good that in their eyes there is in their soul, and forget their past life and their sins of youth and their strayings and follies, and exaggerate their virtues.

and they even praise things that he dislikes: "Nam et contristor aliquando laudibus meis cum vel ea laudantur in me in quibus mihi ipse displiceo vel etiam bona minora et levia pluris aestimantur quam aestimanda sunt." What purity and candor of soul! But Augustine, brilliant in all his conceptions, found a way, also very original, to combat the terrible enemy of vainglory that enters his senses without feeling it and sometimes even without being able to avoid it: discovering before the whole world what he had been before his conversion and what he was at the time of writing the Confessions. No matter how much you exalt me, he comes to tell them, do not forget that I was a lost young man dominated by bad passions, that I was proud and ambitious and that I was, above all, a pest and a mad dog who did not stop for nine years from barking against the Church of God and persecuting her little ones, her unlearned children, with my sophistry. If today I am something else, I am so exclusively by divine grace, by the mercy of God. Praise and exalt, then, with me the Lord, who deigned to have compassion for my misery, and have compassion for it, directing pious prayers to the Most High for me, so that I may be completely free from it, and cease your praises, which bring me no good and can cause me great harm. I want to be loved by you, I want to be esteemed and revered by you; But, for that very reason, I want you to grieve with me for my past and present evils and praise God for my goods, which are His, exclusively His. Esteem me, yes, but not more than I esteem and appreciate myself and how I esteem and appreciate myself. Augustine, upon finishing writing his Confessions, would surely feel satisfied with his pious invention, since without a doubt, when they read his book, friends and enemies would feel great disappointment with that man whom they considered an extraordinary case of science and virtue. See me as I am, I would tell them like Count Dario; Look closely at this portrait of me, drawn by my own hand. Take a good look at me again and again and do not praise me or think more highly of me than I am. By myself I descended to the bottom of the abyss, to the most abject and ridiculous part of error and sin; By the grace of God I am what I am. If you find anything good in me, do not attribute it to me, but to God, who has given it to me: "Ipsi gloria et honor."

For the first time in History, the strange case occurred that a man at the height of his glory wrote a book about his intimate and sinful life, confessing out loud to the face of the world and taking God as a witness of the truth of his confession. From that moment his life of sin and straying,

perhaps known to very few outside of their families, it will be the domain of everyone. Everyone will know who Augustine was in his youth, inside and out, because with an unprecedented cruelty he will tell us even his most shameful passions, even his most hidden thoughts, even his most impudent petulances. But—what is surprising!—the book comes out and, as if there had been a pious conspiracy of the people, it breaks out everywhere and provokes a fiery and continuous applause^ and Augustine is praised without reservation for what he says and for the way he says it, and his book is devoured as if it were a work of scandal in our days. The poor Bishop of Hippo no longer has any new resources for humiliation. It only remains for his afflicted and saddened heart to remain silent, suffer and offer God the sacrifice of praise. Once again the saying of the Savior was fulfilled: He who humbles himself will be exalted. It is an unquestionable fact that our psychological and even physiological states significantly influence our appreciations and judgments of things. Aristotle already said that "whatever one receives from the external world is received according to the way of the one who receives it", an adage that our poet translated very elegantly when he said that "everything is the color of the glass with which it is viewed." This is true of daily experience and of universal value, especially when it refers to changes of a moral and religious order, in which feelings and ideas undergo a more profound and radical modification. Actions that in a state of dissipation and spiritual abandonment seemed little less than innocent, later seen through the prism of a living faith burned with love for God, seem like monstrous crimes and sins of extraordinary gravity. When Saint Augustine wrote the Confessions, between the years 398 and 400, his point of view had changed noticeably. On the one hand, it was more than thirty years away from most of the facts and events referred to in them; On the other hand, his psychological and moral state had totally changed. The ecstasy of Ostia shows us that his introduction into the mystical state was, as in Saint Paul, almost instantaneous with his conversion. And if we add to this that the Confessions were written about fifteen years after this one, we will have an approximate idea of ​​the perfection and holiness to which he was elevated at that historical moment, perfection and holiness that the Saint himself has left us reflected in book X of those. Such observations, true and just in principle, have caused many modern critics to raise a sharp question about the historicity of the Confessions. If the events they relate—they say—are so many years away, if Augustine's inner state is totally different from when they took place, have they not suffered a profound modification when they were transferred to paper? Can we be sure that the division he gives us is objective and accurate? The examination of the Dialogues of Cassiciacus—add these sagacious critics—reveals an innumerable number of differences of appreciation and detail that make us vehemently suspicious of their account. Saint Augustine has occasions in the Confessions in which he has been able to lie openly without being noticed, because they were facts witnessed only by him, and yet, he remains faithful to the dictates of his conscience, leaving things in a prudent doubt. When in the garden in Milan he hears the divine voice telling him Take and read, he does not dare to say that it was a voice from heaven, but rather a voice like that of a boy or girl coming from the neighboring house. And whoever says this, says many other things in which the Saint takes an extremely circumspect attitude. Lying, even for pious purposes and spiritual edification? This is inconceivable in San Agustín. If any man totally identified with the truth, it was Augustine. Throughout his life he never ceased to cry out against lies, whose malice he knew and exposed in vivid colors never seen before. God is truth, and only with the truth can he be worthily honored. Only the father of lies can please the lie. Saint Augustine feels a true horror, an almost infinite hatred, of lies.

By this time of the Confessions he had already written his book De mendacio, in which he maintains the thesis of the absolute illegality of lying, even a slight one, and this even if it is to save the world.

However, no one accuses him of this fault, no one doubts what he says, even if someone misinterprets what he says. But Saint Augustine goes further in his guarantees of veracity. His Confessions are not an impersonal and abstract autobiography, a desktop work and self-apology, as we have already indicated. The Confessions are a work of divine praise and of Christian and painful confession, made in the presence of God, whom he takes as a witness of the truth of the things he narrates. And he repeats this to us a hundred times and with a monotonous and constant rhythm, as if he were afraid that he would forget or the reader might suspect something else. The Confessions of Saint Augustine have the accent of one; sacred effusion, of a solemn oath repeated in the presence of God and men. No matter how little virtue, no matter how small the flame of faith was in him, in such conditions and with such guarantees it is not possible to doubt the good faith and sincerity of the account of the Confessions. Prospero Alfaric himself, a man little suspected of partiality, recognizes Augustine's sincerity and testimonial rectitude: "Augustine," he says, "is not in the habit of speaking against his conviction" 2J. But couldn't passion—as this same author affirms—prevent the Saint from seeing things correctly? Couldn't a doctrinal or theological concern be the cause of unconscious inaccuracies!?

With the best good will in the world and with unquestionable sincerity, see the things of your past with different eyes than they really were, thus making them fit into the picture of your concerns about grace and justification? There is no doubt—and we have already said it—that a strong passion, and much more so if it is of a religious nature, can color the memory of our past actions with its color. But what is possible in general must be demonstrated in particular; That is, the existence of such theological or religious passion or concern must be proven in each case. To act otherwise is to go against the laws of History and Criticism and turn one and the other into a pure game of imagination and whim. Saint Augustine, it is true, perhaps paints with too bright colors human misery, its incapacity for any good work, without the grace of God, and the corruption of our nature; but this has its excuse and explanation after one's own and others' experience, too painful and regrettable not to leave a deep mark on one's soul. The Confessions are, it is true, a fiery exaltation, a rapturous and magnificent song to divine grace, without which nothing good can or can be achieved by human nature, whose perversion and weakness perhaps exaggerated by a natural contrast. But deep down, more than this, the Confessions are a vibrant hymn to the mercy and gratuity of the grace of God, who, far from hating man for his sins and miseries, pities him, requests him and calls him, and when he surrenders to him, showers him with graces and favors. That is the reason why the words mercy and misery, love and compassion, medicine and illness, constantly come to his pen and he takes so much pleasure in remembering the parables of the lost sheep, the prodigal son, the family man and all those that speak to us with tender accents of God's endearing love for men. And all this is said by the Saint in the presence of God, as a calm and sweet meditation, without passion or disturbance; like a spontaneous confidence that flows from his heart, overflowing with gratitude towards God, to whom he owes all the good of his soul; as a firm and heartfelt doctrinal exposition of certain truths, acquired, yes, at the cost of much work and suffering, but whose possession he now enjoys safely and in peace.

If the Confessions had been written twelve years later, the passion of the Pelagian struggle would have given reasons for suspicion on the matter. But around 400 the question of grace had not yet raised the slightest contradiction. It is true that in the Pelagian controversy Saint Augustine appeals several times to the testimony of his Confessions; but it is never in shape

as a reply, but as proof of the impartiality and independence of his doctrine, expressed many years before in its general lines with the same accuracy and clarity as if he had written it years later, fought by Pelagius and his supporters. Saint Augustine is a staunch defender of the gratuitousness of divine grace and mercy, because he knows very well what he would have been without them, abandoned to his own strength. But this feeling that emerges ardent and impetuous in all the pages of his Confessions does not show the slightest clash of combat, the slightest exaggeration of controversy, the slightest proselytizing passion. But Saint Augustine, no matter how unobservant he was, when looking at his historical past, could not help but notice the merciful hand of the Lord, who, without him knowing it, and often against his own will and intention, guided and led him to the port of faith and the bosom of the Catholic Church. That he had this vision after he was converted and not before? Evident. But neither is the reality of the fact any less. Does not the young man who frequently sees himself displeased and repressed by his father in his whims and ravings become angry and enraged against him and protest against his strictness, which he fails to understand? When the years pass and the maturity of judgment comes to him, and with it the sense of reality, he will understand the righteousness of his father's views and the love he had for him by not letting him go down crooked paths, which would have led him to misery and perdition. Shall we say about him that because his vision of the facts and his judgment of his father's behavior have changed, that the latter is not more just and real than the first? Saint Augustine examines in detail, it is true, his life from an entirely different and supernatural point of view, such as his conversion, and sees that most of the events that make up that life are leading him, without him knowing it, to that happy end. The facts that it refers to as realities and as phenomena of consciousness are within the reach of any observant spirit. The finalist interpretation given may be discussed, but never completely invalidated, if the reasons or principles on which it is based are solid and conclusive. It is true that knowledge of the value of a fact does not change it with a new vision of it; But it is also true that the new vision of it does not make it change reality, if it is sufficiently contrasted.

Admitting the supernatural fact of the Saint's conversion, it is logically necessary to admit that Saint Augustine could not have had any interest in distorting the facts, since by one way or another he had to supernaturally reach it, since God uses human facts to prepare the soul for the final blow of grace.

The most compelling proof, however, of the historicity of the Confestones is offered by the silence of all its enemies on this point. Neither Manichaeans, nor Donatists, not even the Pelagians, to whom his Confessions did so much harm, ever fought against the historicity and truthfulness of those, despite the fact that both tried to abuse his stories to discover, if not the falsity of what was referred to, but the reality or existence of things that he left unsaid and that they believed they glimpsed. The Saint calls as a witness to the truth of his Confessions all the sensible and prestigious men who lived then and had known him in his youth = \ That the Saint does not relate each and every one of the events of his past life? It's obvious. The Confessions are not a diary of his life. Neither was anyone interested in knowing it in detail. The Dialogues of Casiciaco have preserved for us pictures and references that completely silence the Confessions. And the same can be said of many of his letters and some of his pamphlets written around this time, in which he has left us interesting data about his life, but which do not make up his Confessions. For the biographer of the Saint, the Concessions constitute a very important and first-rate source, but not the only one. Whoever wanted to stick exclusively to those would leave the life of the Saint largely mutilated, and not in what is less interesting and sublime. Let's conclude on what has been said. The Confessions of Saint Augustine are not a rigorous autobiography, but they are a rigorously historical work, both when it speaks against itself and when it speaks in its favor. Saint Augustine is an essentially sincere temperament and a friend of the truth. When he writes his Confessions he is already at the heights of holiness. He knows well, furthermore, that God hates nothing like lies. Therefore, neither by humiliating nor exalting himself would Augustine be capable of the slightest betrayal of the truth. If at times one finds in his Confessions phrases of extreme abasement, declaring himself the most sinful of men, an abyss of corruption or a monster of iniquity, these phrases have no more meaning in him than they have in the mouths of the saints, which imply only a partial and relative aspect of objective reality. In the Confessions we must also distinguish the fact from the comment. Saint Augustine usually exposes the fact in a concise and rigorous manner, and then expands on it in broad and subtle comments.

Of course it cannot be denied that between the Dialogues of Cassiciacus and the Confessions there are notable differences of substance and form, which is perhaps what gave rise to the opinion cited. Firstly, there is a considerable period of time between the writing of one and the other. The environment, the circumstances of place and time, age, company, everything is different. Surely his writings had to reflect different environments and situations. The inner moods are also different. In Cassiciacus, Augustine is still strongly impressed by Platonic philosophy; he has just left the Milan professorship; He finds himself before a group of disciples whom he has to exercise in the management of philosophy and poetry: they are all young, they all long for wisdom, truth and beauty; They are all dominated by enthusiasm for the liberal arts, for the conquest of the supreme and non-perishable ideal of science and virtue. Augustine necessarily had to reflect this atmosphere, half philosophical, half bucolic, of the Brianza countryside, intermingled with tears, prayers, sighs and penances, with its share of poetry, contemplation of nature and mystical elevation towards God. If the Dialogues did not truly reflect this atmosphere of Christianity and Platonism, of philosophy and poetry, of prayer and discussion, we would be vehemently suspicious of their veracity. The Confessions, on the contrary, are written in a totally ecclesiastical and sanctity environment. Augustine is now a bishop.

VIII MAIN EDITIONS OF THE «CONFESSIONS»

There are many Latin and Castilian editions that have been made of the Confessions, and some of them are of notable perfection. Since it is impossible to list them all, we will only mention the main ones in both languages. a)

The first of the Latin letters that appeared was in Strasbourg, in 1469, in Gothic letters, in the printing press of Juan Mentelin. Six years later a new one appeared in Milan, without the name of the publisher. But really the first careful one and with some critical air was that of Basel in 1489, in J. Amerbach. In 1502, the one from Paris, by J. Bodio, was published, which was followed very shortly after by that of Erasmus of Rotterdam, which notably improved the text of the previous editions. But the one prepared by the so-called Lovanian Theologians (Th. Gozaeo and J. Molano), published in the years 1576-1577, in Antwerp, in the printing press of the famous editor Plantino, easily defeated them all. In the middle of the 17th century, the renowned Jansenist Antonio Arnauld, doctor of the Sorbonne, published a new one, made with great care and competence in view of numerous and important codices, which represented a great step forward in the purification of the text. A few years later the Benedictines of San Mauro printed the complete edition of the works.

In 1930, on the occasion of the 15th centenary of the death of Saint Augustine, a manual edition was published in El Escorial, which attempted, at the same time to spread the reading of this precious work among the clergy and learned people, to offer a new text that was more refined and correct than the existing ones. The procedures followed for this were two entirely new principles and in themselves safe and effective, namely: the principle or theory of rhythm and the principle of comparison of the various families of codices with the fragments called eugypianos. Theory of rhythm.—The theory of rhythm, based on what the Saint says in book IV De doctrina christiana, consists of the continuous or very frequent use of certain rhetorical figures about the harmony of language, which Quintilian already speaks of in his Oratory Institutions as an invasive corruption. In Africa, especially, it became so dominant that many of the sermons and treatises of the writers of the fourth and fifth centuries seem more like rhymed prose than anything else. Saint Augustine himself felt strongly attracted by this decadent music of rhythm, and even seems in a certain sense to canonize it when he says: "Ego in meo eloquio quantum modeste fieri arbitror non praetermitto istos numeros classularum" 3. And that he does not omit them his works bear good testimony.

What should be noted in advance is that the rhythm in our Saint is very biblical, undoubtedly due to the constant reading of the Psalms. We can reduce this rhythm to three fundamental classes: conceptual rhythm, periodic rhythm and verbal rhythm. Of these three, the conceptual is divided into synthetic, when the thoughts are completed; antithetical, when they are opposed, and tautological, when they are repeated with different words or metaphors. Finally, the verbal rhythm can be paranomassic or agnominatio (word games), homeoteleutic or similidesinente. Saint Augustine observes with great scrupulosity this law of parallelism, subject to that of symmetry, whether antithetical or synthetic, in which he found an ornament of singular language: "Totus fere locus," he writes of Saint Paul, whose antitheses and parallelisms delighted him greatly, "temperatum habet elocutionis genus, ubi illa pulchriora sunt in quibus propria propriis tanquam debita reddita decenter excurrunt»'. The various manifestations of parallelism, whether verbal, conceptual or phraseological, are so simple that they are not worth even stopping to enumerate. Rhyme.—Here is another very important element of our Saint's style. Rhyme, in one form or another, has always existed and in all peoples. Rome has preserved excellent examples for us in the song of the Arvales brothers, in the Euguvinian Tables, in the prayer that a father of families addresses to Mars, preserved in Cato 8, etc., etc. Saint Augustine—and even more than him the African writers who followed him—feels an innate propensity toward this figure, which the Latin classics always viewed with a certain caution and antipathy. The final rhyme, above all, had to sound in his ears, accustomed to syllabic quantity, like an unpleasant hammering and singing. But the African ears, which, as the Saint says, did not understand or cure syllabic quantities or defective pronunciations, "felt a certain pleasure in this manifestation of rhythm, which gave the phrase a solemn, rhythmic and harmonious movement. Saint Augustine uses and abuses this figure in his Sermons to the People, but he also uses it on a large scale in the Confessions, a work with an intimate and familiar flavor, so to speak." The final rhyme is, without a doubt, the most common in them; but in addition to this it admits another or others within the phrase, which German critics call multiple rhyme (Mehrfacher Reim). See an example of it: «Cito sonuerunt exultutione, qui videbant eum—et cyto siluerunt inten/ione, ut mdirent eum» ". So perfect is the correspondence here that a single syllable that is deleted breaks the parallelism and symmetry.

In addition to these manifestations of literary rhythm, which should not be confused with the assonance or final consonance, also called rhyme, other figures occur very frequently in the Saint, such as alliteration, repetition of a letter; anadiplosis, repetition of a word or a short phrase; anaphora, repetition of a word at the beginning of each member; gradation, when the last word of one member is the first of the next, etc. To what has been said above we must add three other elements of great importance for textual criticism and that make up, so to speak, the main axis of the theory of rhythm: parallelism, rhyme and games of words and sounds. The parallelism or symmetrical correspondence of the different members of a phrase and of these among themselves, abounds exceedingly in the works of Saint Augustine, particularly in the Confessions. Parallelism consists of distributing words in two or more phrases or phrase members, in such a way that they form equal and symmetrical groups that correspond to each other up to the same number of syllables, and, if possible, that end in syllables of the same sound. The codices support both lessons; editors, for the most part, lean toward the first. But, according to our rhythmic principle, the second must be adopted, reading it in this way; Metuebam ¡taque credere «in carne natum» ne credere cogerer «ex carne inquinatum».

Allow us to add a third dubious lesson. The editors all read, with the exception of Knoell, responsis instead of responsionibus. The manuscript tradition is on its side, since only the Sesorian reads responsionibus. But, according to our law of rhythm, it must also be read like this, even if all the other codices are against it: Absit ut tu workshops eam in illis "visiondbus" et "responsionibus."

As the discreet reader can observe, the variant lessons claimed by the law of rhythm are more acceptable, which are commonly defended by the Maurinos, the best connoisseurs of the style and language of the great Hippo Doctor to date. The other new principle of criticism that we used was the comparison of the different families of the codices with the fragments of Eugipio. This author, from Africa and a disciple of Saint Augustine, lived for a long time in a monastery of Lucullus, near Naples, after his expulsion from African soil by the vandals. Enthusiastic and extremely devoted to his holy Founder and Father, and knowledgeable of his works like no other, he made a kind of florilegium of them, in which he included eight extensive fragments of the Confessions '\ Both due to the antiquity of the author and the codex used by him, prior to all known ones, his testimony had to be of great weight as a comparative element. If some amendments and errors had been introduced in the codices of the Confessions by copyists or recensionists, it was not easy for these corrections and errors to have been extended to the florilegium of Eugipius. The testimony, then, of this author seems to be immune from any intentional manipulation by their amanuenses. He could, therefore, be an excellent and impartial judge among the diversity of families in the codices of our book. Of course, it is already evident in many families that their variant lessons are of relatively modern origin; Carolingian period, in which a recension had to be made. But since the Sesoriano on the one hand and the remaining codices on the other were found very frequently, the important and fundamental thing in this case was to know which lessons should prevail: those of the Sesoriano and its derivatives or those of the other codices called Maurinos. It was the only way out of the impasse that previous critics and editors had found themselves in. The result of the comparison was highly fruitful and interesting. When the Sesoriano was accompanied by some other codex, particularly O, Eugipio supported its reading; When he was alone, he coincided with the others. This led us to establish the following practical principles of criticism: I. When the Sesorian is alone against all the others, the lesson of the latter must prevail against the former. II. When the Sesorian is supported by any of these, his lesson must be considered good, as long as the contrary is not clear. III.

If the Sesoriano is supported only by some codices of Eugipio, particularly by Vaticanus 3,375, its reading must be considered good. These fragments are the following: 1.9 Il, l..., I 5,6 (tuo). 2.eX 6.8 (done)..., X 6.10 (terra). 3.eX 24.35..., X 34.53 (meoí useful). 4th X 41.69 (tu es v.)..., X 43.69 (tu vobis). 5.9 XI 23,29 (dona)..., X 24,31 (non solum). 6.» III 27,34 (ergo nec)..., XI 31,41 (tu es). 7.» XII 25.34..., XII 25.35 (I will expose). 8.* XII 27,37... The lessons supported by the Sesoriano, Eugipio and codices or any of them must be considered genuine. Supported by these two principles, that of rhythm and the comparison of codices, we have believed to resolve a not small series of fluctuating lesson variants in the editions up to this point for no other reason than the taste and whim of their authors. The fact that the vast majority of the lessons proposed in our edition were adopted, as well as the critical principles on which we were based, is the best proof of the goodness of the procedures followed. Spanish editions

The Confessions of Saint Augustine were among his works that were first translated into Spanish, except for The City of God. The first version that was given to the print was that of Father Toscano, made with too much adherence to the letter and in a language that was not entirely traditional and fluent. It has, however, the glory of having been used by Saint Teresa, who speaks of it in her Life. This was followed by that of Father Rivadeneira, written in classic and elegant language, which is why for a long time it was the most read of all. Rivadeneira's translation is often very uneven, sometimes sticking too close to the letter and other times also paraphrasing too much. Furthermore, it does not always express the original text exactly. In 1723 a new version appeared in Madrid, due to the pen of Father Gante, an Augustinian, which achieved great acceptance among the scholarly public, meriting more than seven editions being made of it in a short time. Father Gante improved the style of Father Toscano and made the Holy Patriarch speak in Spanish; but it was very far from offering the perfection that could be desired and expected from his learned pen. Despite its defects, it can be said that it was the most read and edited in its century and part of the next until Father Zeballos's came. Father Zeballos, a learned man, a great connoisseur of Latin and Spanish, a correct and often elegant writer, possessed of
Main editions

more of French, which he mastered, among other languages, to perfection, he decided to make a new translation that would once and for all obviate all the drawbacks of the previous translations! This father also had the good fortune to stumble upon the magnificent French translation and Latin edition of the Benedictine P. J. I. Martín, which he knew how to take advantage of to marvel. Even the prologue itself is almost all of it translated into Father Martín's handwriting. With such a good teacher, it is not surprising that Father Zeballos's translation far surpassed all the previous ones. Written in good Spanish, and usually very faithful and exact in terms of meaning, it is read with real pleasure, and for many years it has enjoyed well-deserved popularity. In reality, for the pious public, who does not stop at trifles nor looks for anything other than the thought of the Saint, no other than this should be printed. Its main defect is being paraphrase or free, which today constitutes a serious drawback for scholars and scholars who want a literal or the most literal possible. Responding to these desires or tendencies, we decided to undertake a new translation, with no little work and difficulty, and in times as unfortunate as the beginnings of the ill-fated Spanish Republic. Regarding the criteria followed in the translation, we wrote in the prologue of the first edition the following: «As for the translation, we have always had in view those golden words of my brother in religion, Fray Luis de León, which he left written in front of his translation and commentary on the Song of Songs, and which read as follows: «He who translates must be faithful and complete, and if possible, count the words to give as many and no more nor less, and of the same quality and condition and variety of meanings that the originals have, without limiting them to their own meaning and appearance, so that those who read the translation can understand all the variety of meanings that the original gives rise to, if it were read, and are free to choose from them the one that seems best to them... Hence it may be that some are not so happy and it seems that in some parts the reason falls short, being able to very easily remedy it by changing some words and adding others, which I did not do, because I understand the job to be different from the one that translates "of the one who explains and comments."

Such is the criterion that we have followed in our translation, sticking as closely as possible to the text and making it adjust "and respond to it—as the author himself says—not only in the sentences and words, but even in the concert and air of them, imitating their figures and ways of speaking, as much as is possible in our language." Whether we have achieved it or not is irrelevant.

For many of the notes we have used the Cambridge edition of GibbMontgomery and the Oxford edition of Pusey; for the vast majority we have used our studies on the subject, to which we frequently refer the reader. Although we could have considerably increased the number of these, we have stuck to those strictly necessary. In them we have mainly attended to scholars and writers, an audience often forgotten in this type of works, giving rise to all those mystical and moral considerations, typical of a devout edition, and which would extraordinarily increase the volume. However, we believe that even devout people will benefit from these erudite notes, all of which are aimed at making the text of the Holy Zo more intelligible. After our version, two other new translations have come to light: that of the priest Lorenzo Riber and that of the Apostolate of the Press. That of Don Lorenzo Riber, which appeared in 1942 in M. Aguilar, with great luxury of presentation, is a literary translation full of life and traditionalism, although at times it avoids the lyrics a bit. He also resents certain influences from the French version of Labriolle, whose Latin text he proposed to follow. All in all, it is a translation that deserves to be read and enjoyed by all true lovers of good literature and devotees of this admirable book by the great Bishop of Hippo. It also has an extensive and brilliant introduction, in which he masterfully presents a sympathetic and lavish portrait of the Saint. He has intentionally avoided all discussion and erudite notes that could distract the reader from savoring the pages of this work, all light and color, all passion and sublime lyricism that the soul must taste alone in the secrecy and silence of all science and erudition.

That of the Apostolate, by Father Valentín Gómez, is less brilliant and classic in its style, but it is, on the other hand, more faithful to the letter, to which it sometimes adheres too narrowly. It includes only the first eleven books, as it is intended for the pious and simple public, who are only interested in the person of the Saint, not his great philosophical or scriptural speculations. Father Valentín's work is done with true affection, and in many difficult passages he has been able to fully triumph over Latin and the thought of the Saint. It is a translation that, due to its great fidelity to the letter, will always deserve to be consulted by all who intend to make a new one. Ours, which we present to the public again today, is a complete recast of the one we published in 1932. There are books that come out completely new. We have adjusted it even more to the letter; We have made up for the numerous omissions and printing errors that escaped then, and we have divided it into shorter paragraphs, in order to avoid the monotony of the chapters and give more clarity to the Saint's thought. On the other hand, we have suppressed the titles of these, which serve no purpose in this type of edition except to take up space and embarrass the reader. Taking into account that the present edition should be read more by scholars and scholars than by the common people, we have adjusted our notes to this public, although, since the Latin text has a critical apparatus, it has been necessary to refer them, as in the first edition, to the Appendices. May God bless this work of ours, in which we have spent many vigils, so that it may come out less unworthy of the general public, to whom it is directed, and of the great Doctor of the Church, to whom we fervently dedicate it. In our critical apparatus we constantly cite and use the first three editions; the last five only in isolated cases. However, when the device uses the. acronym edds. = editions, we include them too, just as when we say edd. modd. — modern editions. By simply reading the critical apparatus you can deduce the meaning of several of the abbreviations we use. However, for greater clarity we are going to put them here: codds, = all the codices, except S; coded. = the majority of codices, outside those expressly cited; edds. = all ancient and modern editions; Edd. = the old editions and even some modern ones. Regarding this edition we must say that it is completely corrected and retouched in numerous parts. After a constant study of more than twelve years on the text of the Confessions, we believe we have reached solidly proven and, as far as we are concerned, definitive conclusions. We've taken a lot of the guesswork out of it; but we have frequently relegated them to the critical apparatus, respecting the text offered by the codices. For the first time the reading reddens debita... donans debita (I 4,4) is admitted, changing the punctuation, making it an excellent lesson. We have also included for the first time the me mineris reading of the CS codices, which all the editors, because they read memineris, rejected. We also introduce lesson I 5,6, offendat instead of offendant, since when the subject of a sentence in Saint Augustine is feminine and the verb subjunctive, the quae is instead of quod, as can be alleged in countless cases: the manuscript tradition is very authoritative BGS and Eugipio. Likewise in I 8,13 we accept the variant of the HOST codices ceteroque for ceterorumque, because it makes perfect sense and is required by the authority of the codices. In book III 5,9, we read confectam instead of compertam, which offer codices of lower note and that make worse sense. For the same reason, in book VIII 4,9 we read plures instead of plus in the second paragraph. In the same book, 10.25, we score differently, we believe correctly, with S and some other codices; and in number 26 vanitatium, because that is how first-note codices, such as CDOS, bring it, and so they read in book X number 20: cupiditatium. Finally, so as not to tire our readers, in book XIII 11,12 we read for the first time quae, cumque de illa loquitur, scit quid loquitur.

We introduce many other variants and new lessons, which we hope will be accepted by sensible and mature critics. In reality we have done nothing more than be logical in our deductions from established critical principles. For the sake of our readers, we have simplified the critical apparatus as much as possible, leaving only those variants that establish a text different from that of the Maurinos, so that they can appreciate and explain the diversity of texts.

According to Saint Augustine and the ancients, life is divided into seven periods or ages: childhood, which goes from birth to seven years; childhood, from seven to fourteen; adolescence, from fourteen to twenty-eight; youth, from twenty-eight to fifty; virility, from fifty to sixty; old age or senescence, from sixty to eighty, and decrepitude, until death. Corporal punishment, particularly that of canes, straps and canes, was widely used and recommended by teachers, who, adherents of the adage "the letter enters with blood", tended to sin more by excess than by defect, sometimes going as far as the shedding of blood. The punishment of the rod, of which antiquity has preserved eloquent testimony in the mural painting preserved in the Naples Museum, was one of the most cruel. The small victim, held in the air by his feet and hands, had to endure a shower of sticks on his back until he fell half lifeless. These were not, however, the only punishments. Saint Augustine tells us in one of his Sermons (70,2,2) about the confinements and vigils that were sometimes imposed on them. We do not know that the Saint was a victim of such brutal treatment; but the very bitter tone with which he speaks about them and the unfavorable portrait he makes of his teachers lead us to suspect that they are. The phrases and comparisons he uses could not be harsher and more realistic. It was the same for all Latins, who never judged it as anything other than the occupation of unemployed and argumentative people: that of sophistic and idle Greeks. The allegorical explanation of the Old Testament, particularly of the lives of the patriarchs, provided great benefit to Augustine, making him see reasonable what had previously seemed absurd to him. Divine anthropomorphism also found a rational and fair explanation in the Bishop of Milan. In the presence of Ambrose, Augustine saw the enormous edifice of his anti-Catholic prejudices collapse. He had been made to believe that Catholicism was typical of little women and rustics and he found it incarnated in a wise, eloquent, noble man, honored by all the great powers of the earth, starting with the emperors, who obeyed and venerated him as a father and teacher. This was Ambrose's main work with Augustine and almost the only one. Saint Ambrose, in fact, does not seem to care much or little about this young Numidian, quarrelsome and unrepentant arguer, and by all accounts Manichean. He avoids being treated alone, making him wait in the anteroom until he has to leave, bored. He never admitted his friendship. When he needed to open his heart, he had to confide in Simplicianus, a holy and loving man. Still in the solitudes of Cassiciaco, the Saint regrets not having been able to open his heart to him (Soliloquios). Ambrose had to know several of his writings and even the aura of holiness and wisdom of his spiritual son.

But in his works there is not the slightest reference to the young African Doctor. As for Augustine, whenever he speaks of him he does so with veneration and praise and calls him a saint. Note, however, that Augustine then was no more than a little foreign professor with many pretensions and vanity. In De useful, credendi HIV 20, the Saint gives a magnificent description of the state of mind that overwhelmed him at this time, and which can be considered as a preview or outline of this chapter of the Confessions. Because then I could have found myself very fit and docile if there had been someone to instruct me. These last words seem like a lament for the abandonment, inadvertent or intentional, in which the Bishop of Milan had him, to whom more than once he wanted to confide the concerns and doubts of his heart, without succeeding, and which he still laments in Soliloquies 11 14,26. The Romans had three types of public games, included in the common name of shows: those of the circus, those of the amphitheater and those of the theater. The first, called circuses of the place, were those that took place when men fought with others, either by means of animals: horse races, chariots, etc.; either directly with each other, such as gladiators, those condemned to death, etc. Those in the amphitheater were fights between men and beasts, something similar to our bulls, although with all kinds of beasts: lions, tigers, panthers, etc. Those in the theater were performed by actors, imitating the nefarious actions of the gods. It is not easy to explain the fury and ardor that the first two, and above all, the circus performers, aroused in the savage, bloodthirsty mobs of the Roman people. Augustine, a delicate soul and above all a convinced and practical Manichean, hated those two with all his soul because of the deaths that were always in them, at the same time that he gave himself fully to them, as we saw previously (III 11,2). «There are mainly two – says the Saint – the attractions of the Manichaeans with which they catch the unwary: one, when they rebuke the Scriptures, both those who misunderstand and those who want to misunderstand; another, leading an apparently chaste and continent life” (De mor. manich. It is almost certain that the Saint is referring to Ennead V, where he speaks of the divine hypostases according to Plato. The Plotinian conception is the following: the first substance is the One (Enn. V 1,6). From this substance proceeds by eternal generation and without alteration of the begetter the Mind or Nous, image of the One (Enn. V 1,7). The Nous engenders the universal Soul (ib., 1,7).

According to Plotinus, the Mind and the One are equal, distinguished by their decay of being, the One being more perfect, then the Nous and finally the Soul, until ending in Matter. Plotinus attributes his trinity to Plato, but it is only found in Plato as a reference put into the mouth of Parmenides. According to him, the One only engenders the Nous, and is the source of everything; Nous is the creator of all things, including the universal Soul, which, in turn, engenders Matter. The One is light by essence, shining within and above human minds; all other beings are enlightened, etc. (Enn. VI 1,8). These Enneads, perhaps translated paraphrastically and in the Catholic sense, must have overwhelmed Augustine with enthusiasm, when he compared them with the prologue of the Gospel of Saint John. He commands, I say, that he wants—and he would not command if he did not want to—and, nevertheless, he does not do what he commands. Therefore he does not want completely; Therefore, it does not rule all of it; because insofar as it commands whatever it wants, and insofar as it does not do what it commands in so far as it does not want, because the will commands whatever will it is, and no other than itself. The traditio and redditio symboli was a ceremony of the ancient Church that took place days before baptism. In Africa, the traditio or delivery of the symbol used to take place fifteen days before Easter, on Passion Sunday. If someone had not learned it, it was extended for eight more days: from Passion Sunday to Holy Saturday. If you didn't know then you were rejected. It is curious that Petrarch refers to this purpose in one of his letters (Famil. IV 1) to his brother Francis Dionysius. Having climbed one day with his younger brother to the top of Mount Windy, not without great fatigue, after recreating his view with the magnificent panorama he discovered and having contemplated the Alps, the province of Lyon and the course of the Rhône and The Gulf of Marseilles, he pulled out the copy of the Confessions of Saint Augustine, which he always carried with him, and managed to open them to this chapter and place. Taking the lesson to himself, he closed the book, and angry with himself for going to contemplate earthly things, having in his soul so many wonders to admire, he descended from the mountain without speaking a word to his brother. Saint Augustine divided the objects of the understanding into sensible and intelligible, in the style of Plato, and Neoplatonists. In all these chapters of the Confessions Saint Augustine exposes everything that can be said about memory as a faculty, as an act and as a psychological phenomenon, and in a methodical way. Saint Augustine distinguishes here with great sagacity between curiosity and pleasure, however, it cannot be denied that the satisfaction of curiosity, even with objects that do not cause delight, such as a destroyed corpse, a monster or something similar, produces its pleasure, consisting of the satisfaction of a desire. Saint Augustine, an observant spirit, felt captivated by the habits of animals, of which he had a knowledge that was not vulgar and for the most part direct. The examples he cites here are vulgar, but revealing of his analytical and scrutinizing genius. It will seem strange to many that a wise man and a saint like Saint Augustine sometimes suspends his pen and the most serious occupations and becomes engrossed in contemplating the efforts of the stellion in catching a fly or the efforts of the spider in imprisoning its prey. And yet, these small episodes reveal more healthy humanism than many of their great speculations. Augustine found in these small things no less greatness and wisdom of God than in the great ones, and they served as an alarm clock for him to rise up to God and sing a hymn of praise to Him. The Saint's argument is reduced in a few words to this: the prophet sees future things; but what is not cannot be seen; Therefore these future things exist, and since he sees them in the category of future time, it follows that this obviously exists.

Considering the actions of men as parts of a life, at the same time that individual actions are parts of the integral life of the individual, is one of the most brilliant and fruitful ideas of Saint Augustine, which he develops admirably in his City of God. When speaking about the philosophy of history, it is common, if not exclusive, to consider divine providence as the main element of history, when in reality such a thought is common to all Christian writers. But to consider humanity as one man, as one life, which develops through the centuries under the divine aegis, transmitting from one people to another the torch of civilization and the imperfection disappearing to give rise to the development of a new organism, this, I say, is found for the first time in Saint Augustine, for whom there is only one history, one culture, etc. Phil 3,12. J. Llamas. The testimony, although it has given play to the theory of multiple literal meaning in the Middle Ages, of which Saint Thomas is a strong champion, who cites the Bishop of Hippo in his favor, does not seem clear to us, much less decisive. Writers on this subject are commonly inclined to believe that Saint Augustine defended the multiple literal meaning. Only Tailon (Recherches de Science Religieuse, January-April 1921, pp.1-28) and Father Llamas (article cit.) have dared to defend the opposite, not without great signs of probability. Father Fernández (in Verbum Domini, 1927, pp.281ff) establishes the following conclusions: « l. s, Augustine never formed a decisive opinion about the multiple literal meaning; 2.", he did not openly reject it; on the contrary, out of charity, he first desired it, then proposed it as an opinion; 3. 5, which, however, he quickly abandoned: 4. a, and, consequently, that it cannot be said that Saint Augustine taught and supported the sentence of multiple literal meaning, and especially if one takes into account that in all his comments he sticks to the literal meaning. » These conclusions of the illustrious Spanish writer must be taken as the minimum of concessions, and the first affirmative opinion must be rejected. In this chapter the Saint changes the middle ground, abandoning the hypothesis of multiple literal meanings and proposing that of multiple true or rather probable meanings, since the Saint speaks of many and diverse ones that can allege scriptural evidence in their favor. Do not forget that the Saint's thought is not to resolve the question of multiple literal meanings, but rather to reconcile the different opinions that existed among Christians on a multitude of points in Scripture; and in this sense the solution given in this last chapter is more expeditious and affordable, and the great Doctor appeals to it as a last resort.

This statement destroys the opinion of those who maintain that the Saint defended the plurality of the literal meaning. He outlines the same rule of conduct for us in De Gen. ad litt., I 21,41: «When we read the sacred books and there are a multitude of true interpretations, we choose primarily the one that seems to be the one intended by the author we read; If this does not appear clear..., the one that has the Catholic faith as its support and agrees with hearing passages of the same Scripture.» And in De doctr. christ. III 27,380, insists on the same thing: "The interpreter of the Holy Scriptures must work hard," he says, "to find the intention of the sacred writer, through whom the Holy Spirit dispensed said Scripture to us," etc.

Which of my pamphlets has spread more widely and is read more frequently and with more pleasure than my Confessions? Well, having published them before the Pelagian heresy appeared, I certainly said in them and repeatedly: "Give what you command, and command what you want." Receive the books you wanted from my Confessions. See me in them, so that you do not praise me more than I am. Believe me in them, not what others say about me.
